questions.scenario: A user is creating a password for a new social media account.
questions.hint: Look for the most common, predictable patterns found in every password leak.

candidates.explanation: While predictable, it is slightly stronger than a generic default password due to capitalization and symbols.
Similar to BlueDog-55, it provides slightly more resistance than common defaults.
A simple combination of words and numbers that is harder to guess than 'password123'.
This is one of the most common passwords globally and is the first thing an attacker's script will try.

questions.scenario: An employee is setting up their login for the 'GlobalTech' corporate portal.
questions.hint: Attackers often target 'Corporate' patterns: CompanyName + Year + SpecialChar.

candidates.explanation: This is a 'passphrase'. Even without symbols, the length provides significant protection against brute force.
Though it uses common substitutions, it's less predictable than the specific company-branded pattern.
This follows a highly predictable corporate pattern (Company + Year + Symbol) that is trivial for attackers to guess using 'mask attacks'.
A random string of characters provides high entropy and is very difficult to crack.

questions.scenario: A security-conscious user thinks they have created an unbreakable password by using complex substitutions.
questions.hint: Complexity (symbols/numbers) is not the same as entropy. Common words with substitutions are easily handled by modern cracking tools.

candidates.explanation: Using a series of random words (Diceware) creates high entropy due to the sheer length of the password.
Similar to the Diceware method, this passphrase is significantly harder to crack than a substituted word.
A truly random alphanumeric string with symbols has high entropy and no predictable pattern.
This is a 'complexity illusion'. It looks strong, but it's just common words with standard substitutions (e=3, a=@, o=0) and a sequence, which crackers handle automatically.
